pf-01.answer: A citation the retriever never returned is a fabrication and should be stripped and flagged.

pf-02.answer: First diagnostic question: did the right passage reach the prompt? If the right passage was present and the answer still went wrong, the failure is in generation: instructions, formatting, or the model ignoring context. If retrieval missed it, fix chunking, the index, or the query instead.

pf-03.answer: A loop that cannot refuse will fabricate. When retrieval returns nothing relevant, the correct behavior is to say so before spending a model call and flag the answer for human review. The refusal path should be designed first because it is the path every other safeguard falls back to.

pf-04.answer: The four parts are Perceive, Decide, Act, and Observe. The application owns Perceive, Act, and Observe; only Decide belongs to the model.

pf-05.answer: The autonomy spectrum ranges from a deterministic chain (no decisions) to a tool-using loop (the model picks tools), a reflection loop (the model critiques its own draft), and multi-agent systems (models delegate to models). The professional habit is to start at the bottom of the spectrum and move up only when a measured failure justifies it.

pf-06.answer: When a case fails, the trace answers the diagnostic question — was it retrieval, tool selection, instruction-following, or formatting? — in minutes. Classify each failure into one of those buckets, fix the biggest bucket first, and add a regression case so the same failure cannot return unnoticed.

pf-07.answer: Prefer code-based checks when the property is mechanical — e.g., did it cite the expected source, did it parse, did it stay under the tool budget — because they are fast, free, and deterministic. Before trusting an LLM-as-judge, inspect its false positives and spot-check it against human labels, since it inherits the judge's own biases and a common failure is an evaluator that passes everything.
